title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree
description: Brute force to optimized: explicit path finding and comparison versus a single combined post-order recursive search.

sections.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree

content.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree

blocks.text: 1. Problem Statement

Problem Summary: Given the root of a binary tree and two of its nodes p and q, find their lowest common ancestor (LCA), the deepest node that has both p and q as descendants (a node is considered a descendant of itself).

blocks.caption: What goes in, what comes out

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Detail"],"rows":[["Input","root, and target values p, q"],["Output","The deepest node that is an ancestor of both p and q"],["Key Insight","A node where p is found in one subtree and q in the other (or the node itself is p or q) is exactly the LCA"],["Constraints","Up to 10^5 nodes, p and q guaranteed to exist in the tree"]]}

blocks.text: 2. Pattern Detection

blocks.content: {"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Deepest node that is an ancestor of BOTH targets\"","A single post-order recursive search, where a node reports itself as the answer the moment both targets are found on opposite branches beneath it"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Understand the Problem

Searching recursively from the root, a node can determine, from its own subtree search results, whether it is the LCA: if p is found somewhere in its left subtree AND q is found somewhere in its right subtree (or vice versa), this node IS the split point where the two paths diverge, exactly the LCA. If a node equals p or q directly, it can immediately report itself, since it could itself be the LCA (a node is its own ancestor).

blocks.title: Analogy: Finding Where Two People's Family Lines Last Overlapped
blocks.text: Picture tracing two people's ancestry up a family tree; the lowest common ancestor is the most RECENT shared relative, found by searching down from the top and noticing the exact point where one person's line goes one direction and the other person's line goes the other direction.

blocks.caption: A node where p is found in one subtree and q in the other IS the lowest common ancestor

blocks.text: 4. Understand with Examples
Example: tree = [3, 5, 1, 6, 2, 0, 8, null, null, 7, 4]
LCA(5, 1) = 3. LCA(5, 4) = 5 (since 4 is in 5's own subtree, 5 is its own ancestor here).
5. How Should We Think?

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: If the current node is null, or equals p, or equals q, it can be returned directly, since finding p or q itself means this node is a candidate for being (or being on the path to) the LCA.

Observation 2: Recursively searching the left and right subtrees for p and q returns whichever of p, q, or a deeper LCA was found in EACH respective side.

Observation 3: If BOTH the left search and the right search return a non-null result, it means p and q were found on OPPOSITE sides of the current node, making the current node exactly the LCA.

Observation 4: If only ONE side returns a non-null result, that result (whatever it is, whether p, q, or a deeper LCA) should simply be passed further up unchanged, since the LCA must lie somewhere along that side.
This leads to a single post-order recursive search, where each node combines its two subtrees' search results to determine whether it is the LCA, or to pass along whichever single result was found.
6. Brute Force Solution
Find the explicit root-to-p path and root-to-q path as two separate lists, then compare them to find the last node they have in common.
Why the code is written this way

items: Explicitly finding both paths and comparing them directly implements the definition of "common ancestor" clearly.
This requires storing two full paths and a separate comparison step, when a single combined recursive search finds the same answer directly.

blocks.text: 7. Analyze the Brute Force

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n) for finding both paths.
Space: O(h) for each path list, O(h) recursion depth.
Limitation: a single post-order search finds the LCA directly, without ever constructing explicit path lists.
8. Optimize the Solution

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: Define lca(node, p, q) recursively: if node is null, or node's value equals p, or node's value equals q, return node directly. Otherwise, recursively search the left subtree and the right subtree. If BOTH searches return non-null, this node is the LCA, return it. Otherwise, return whichever ONE search returned non-null (or null if neither did).
Use a single post-order recursive search, combining subtree results to detect the LCA directly.
9. Optimized Solution
Dry run for LCA(5, 1) in the example tree

blocks.content: {"headers":["Node","Left search result","Right search result","Action"],"rows":[["3 (root)","finds 5 (p)","finds 1 (q)","BOTH sides non-null: 3 IS the LCA"]]}

blocks.text: Why This Works

A node is the LCA precisely when p and q are found on DIFFERENT branches beneath it (including the case where the node itself IS one of p or q, and the other target is found somewhere beneath it); the recursive search correctly detects this by checking whether both the left and right subtree searches succeed simultaneously, and otherwise simply forwards whichever single result was found further up the call stack, since the LCA must reside along that same branch.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), visiting each node once.
Space: O(h) recursion depth.
10. Complexity Comparison

blocks.content: {"headers":["Solution","Time","Space","Interview Recommendation"],"rows":[["Find both paths explicitly, then compare","O(n)","O(h) for two path lists","Correct, but needs extra path storage."],["Single combined post-order search","O(n)","O(h) recursion depth","The expected, elegant solution."]]}

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways
Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Tree is a beautiful example of a single recursive pass doing double duty: searching for targets AND detecting the split point simultaneously.
Common Mistakes

items: Forgetting that a node can be its own ancestor (returning early when the current node equals p or q, without further checking beneath it, is actually correct behavior here, not a bug, since the recursion structure handles it properly).
Incorrectly returning null when only one side finds a result, instead of correctly forwarding that one non-null result upward.

blocks.text: Edge Cases

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","Expected Behavior"],"rows":[["One of p or q is an ancestor of the other","The higher one (the ancestor) is correctly returned as the LCA."],["p and q are on completely different subtrees of the root","The root itself is correctly returned as the LCA."]]}

blocks.text: Interview Tips
Explicitly stating "if both subtree searches succeed, this node is the split point, hence the LCA" demonstrates the elegant core insight clearly and quickly.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: If the interviewer says "find the lowest common ancestor of two nodes in a general binary tree", think: a single post-order recursive search combining both subtrees' results.
Interview Follow-up Questions

items: How would this problem change (and simplify) if the tree were specifically a BINARY SEARCH TREE, letting value comparisons guide the search direction directly?

blocks.text: Pattern Connections

items: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree, a simpler variant exploiting the BST ordering property.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Both approaches cost O(n) time; the combined single-pass search avoids the brute force's extra space for two explicit path lists.
12. Final Summary

items: Pattern: a single post-order recursive search combining subtree results to detect a split point.
Core Idea: a node is the LCA when p and q are found on opposite sides beneath it, or when the node itself is one of the targets.
Space: O(h) for two explicit paths in the brute force, O(h) recursion depth in the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: a single combined search can both find targets AND detect the LCA simultaneously.
Interview Difficulty: a classic, elegant medium-level recursive tree problem.
One line memory trick: both sides found something means this node is the split point.
